## Same acreage, very different price

A 40-hectare farm in Quebec's Montérégie region typically doesn't sell for the same price as a similarly sized farm in a more peripheral region. The gap isn't explained by location alone — several concrete factors, often invisible to a buyer comparing regions for the first time, drive these differences. [Transac-TERRES data](../prix-terres-transac-terres/index.qmd) tracks these gaps over time, but it doesn't replace this regional context.

## Soil quality and consistency

Some regions of Quebec have a higher concentration of better-class agricultural soils, more uniform across large areas, with fewer underperforming zones scattered within a given lot. Land in a region known for consistently good soil quality almost always trades at a premium, regardless of the acreage itself.

## Proximity to processing infrastructure

Distance to crop buyers, processing facilities, or distribution networks directly affects a farm's value. A region where agri-food infrastructure is concentrated lowers transport and logistics costs for the operator, and that gets reflected in what buyers are willing to pay.

## Pressure from non-farm demand

In some areas, proximity to urban centres or residential appeal puts upward pressure on farmland prices, even when the agronomic potential remains comparable to a more remote region. That pressure has nothing to do with the soil's productive capacity — it reflects a parallel demand, often for a use that may eventually be something other than farming.

## A history of drainage investment

A region where subsurface drainage has been installed and maintained more systematically over the decades tends to have more consistent yield capacity across its farms, which lowers the risk a buyer perceives and supports the price. A region with a spottier drainage investment history can show a lower average price, but with much greater variability from one parcel to the next.

## Comparing a region, not just a price

Comparing two regions purely on price per hectare misses the point. Soil, infrastructure, market pressure, and drainage history together explain why two farms that look similar at first glance almost never trade quite the same way.
